findings.title: Interrupted adoption cannot be resumed
findings.description: The flow writes artifacts incrementally (step 5: concept → architecture → existing-state slice plan). Detection's rule 2 says any of these artifacts makes the repo "already planned", and `sq onboard` step 2 says "If the project is greenfield or already planned, adoption doesn't apply." So an adoption that dies after the architecture is written but before the slice plan is indistinguishable from a genuinely planned project, and re-running `sq onboard` refuses to continue. The superseded prompt contract explicitly carried the property "a re-run resumes from whatever artifacts exist"; the amendment drops it without replacement. The doc needs to say what a half-written adoption looks like to detection (e.g. derived architecture with `provenance: derived` and no slice plan) and how the flow resumes, or `sq onboard` will be designed against a flow with no failure recovery.

findings.title: Opt-out precedence masks "already planned"
findings.description: The outcome order checks "Opted out" first and concludes "It is greenfield." A project that opted out and then went through the normal greenfield flow and now holds a concept, architecture and slice plan still reports `greenfield` — the report is factually wrong for a fully planned project, and rule 2 ("already planned") is unreachable for any opted-out project. The report is a read-only JSON contract that `sq onboard` and `cf next` consume; consumers that trust the outcome rather than re-deriving from files will mis-navigate. Opt-out should only resolve the brownfield-vs-greenfield question (rule 3's domain); "already planned" should win over it, or the doc must state which consumers ignore the outcome.

findings.title: Dependencies section asserts pending items that already shipped in the guide
findings.description: "Still pending, both written after cf specifies them in slice design: the retroactive-marker rule, and the naming-conventions entry for the docs map file" is stale against the checked-out `project-documents/ai-project-guide`: `guide.ai-project.brownfield-adoption.md` carries the retroactive-slice marker spec (token format, checked/no-design-or-tasks rules, index ordering, `provenance: derived`), and `file-naming-conventions.md` carries the "Docs Map File" entry for `050-docs-map.{project}.md` (managed block `cf-docs-map`), both recorded in the guide's CHANGELOG. This is the section ai-project-guide and squadron read to sequence their work; telling them to wait for what already exists will stall or duplicate effort.

findings.title: Guide version floor contradicts the amendment, the code, and slice 272
findings.description: The same Dependencies bullet says "cf releases that select the brownfield profile require at least **v0.22.2**", but (a) the amendment removed profile selection from `cf build` entirely, so no cf release "selects the brownfield profile" anymore — the requirement now attaches to the slice-271 prompt-delivery primitive; (b) `packages/core/src/guides/guideMinimum.ts` already pins `MIN_GUIDE_VERSION = '0.22.6'`, above the stated floor; and (c) slice 272 will raise `MIN_GUIDE_VERSION` again for the drop-`cf build` prompt update. Related wording drift in "Guide release coupling": after announcing the fail-fast rule "moves to the prompt-delivery primitive", the retained rule text still reads "cf selects the brownfield profile and the installed guide lacks it, `cf build` fails with a named error" — the amended rule should name the new enforcement point. There is no single stated place where the required guide version for the reworked adoption path is defined.

findings.title: Rework deletes the shipped adoption path before its replacement exists
findings.description: Slices 261–267 shipped a working CF-only adoption path (verified: `packages/core/src/adoption/`, `adoptionNavigation.ts`, and `260-analysis.adoption-verification-runs.md` records passing real-repo runs). The amendment makes 268–270 delete it (`cf build` adoption, adoption state, `cf next` adoption navigation) and 271 delete the probe code, while the replacement — `sq onboard` — is "parked" on another repo's roadmap, and "the CF-only fallback is dropped". After 268–272 land, CF has no adoption path at all until squadron delivers, for an unknown duration. The doc does not state whether 268–272 are gated on a squadron commitment or shipped on trust; that sequencing decision is load-bearing and unstated.

findings.title: Related Work references a review artifact that does not exist in this checkout
findings.description: The link `../reviews/260-review.arch.brownfield-adoption.md` does not resolve — there is no `project-documents/user/reviews/` directory here (only slices reference that directory as a convention). The accompanying claim "All findings are addressed in this revision. F009 is resolved by fixing only the relative order..." is therefore unverifiable against the cited source, and one of the two resolutions described (the F009 relative-order fix) is the sole justification for a design constraint on retroactive entries. Either the review file needs to be present, or the claim should be dropped to what the arch itself states.

findings.title: "Anticipated Slices" still narrates behavior the amendment deletes
findings.description: The section lists shipped slices 260–267 with live-sounding descriptions ("`cf build` selecting the `brownfield-adoption` profile", "Brownfield-aware `cf next`: adoption steps while in progress") that the amendment removes, while the actual future work (268–274) appears only in a one-line note and the slice plan. A cross-repo reader skimming for what to build against can land on deleted behavior. Renaming the section to "Shipped slices (superseded where noted)" and listing 268–274 as the anticipated work would remove the ambiguity. The same pattern applies to the retained "probe contract" and "Original (agreed with ai-project-guide 20261020)" blocks: the live prompt-delivery contract is one paragraph ("Slice 271's design settles how the profile's variables are delivered") sitting under two full superseded contracts.
